analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from cutting retiree health benefits after retirement and forces restoration of benefits already taken away.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Education and the Workforce Committee and its subcommittee for the rest of the two-year Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies had been canceling or shrinking health benefits that workers had been promised for their retirement, often after those workers had already left the job and could no longer do anything about it. This bill would have made it illegal for an employer to reduce a retiree's health benefits after the retirement date, and would have required employers to restore benefits they had already cut — with exceptions for companies facing real financial hardship and a federal program to guarantee loans to help companies pay for restoring benefits. The Labor Department could fine violators. The bill was sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Retirees whose employers cut their promised health coverage after they retired would have gotten those benefits restored — including older retirees whose benefits would go back to 1991 levels — and every future retiree with employer health coverage would have been protected from post-retirement cuts. The Labor Department could have enforced the rule with fines, and employers facing hardship could have gotten federally guaranteed loans to help pay for compliance.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retirees whose health benefits were cut

how_it_helps.text: It bars group health plans from reducing, canceling, or raising the out-of-pocket cost of a retiree's health benefits after the participant retires, and voids any plan language that claims the right to do so.

It orders plan sponsors to restore benefits that were cut after retirement, back to the level in effect immediately before the cut (or to 1991 levels for the earliest retirees), with employers required to notify each affected retiree of what they are owed and how to claim it.

It lets the Secretary of Labor waive the restoration duty only where the employer proves it would face substantial business hardship, and blocks waivers for employers that could have used excess pension assets to fund retiree health but did not.

It gives the Labor Department authority to fine violators up to $20,000 per affected participant, and sets up a loan-guarantee program — capped at $5 billion overall, $5 million per employer — so employers who cannot otherwise borrow can finance the restoration.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that sponsor group health plans, which would have had to restore benefits already cut and keep future retiree benefits intact, with the federal government backstopping up to $5 billion in loans and spending $200 million (plus $10 million for administration) on the guarantee program.

drawbacks.text: The restoration requirement is retroactive: employers would have to undo benefit cuts made before the law existed, in some cases restoring coverage to 1991 levels for the oldest retirees, a cost some companies would struggle to absorb.

The bill acknowledged this burden: it allowed sponsors to escape restoration by proving the requirement was unworkable and would cause substantial business hardship, and it created a federal program guaranteeing up to $5 billion in private loans to employers to help pay for restoration, with $200 million in new spending authorized.
Plans with fewer than 100 participants were excluded from the restoration mandate, so retirees of small employers — where benefits are often most fragile — got no help.

Enforcement would have meant new civil penalties of up to $20,000 per affected participant and a wave of administrative proceedings and litigation between retirees and their former employers over whether a given change counted as a prohibited reduction.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit was real: retirees who worked decades for promised health coverage, and who often cannot replace it on the private market because of age or illness, would have gotten their benefits back, and future retirees would have been shielded from the same bait-and-switch. The cost was also real: the bill reached backward, forcing employers to undo cuts made before the law existed, which is a large and unpredictable liability for companies that relied on reserved rights to amend their plans — a burden the bill itself acknowledged by writing a hardship waiver and a federal loan-guarantee program into it. The hardship waiver (requiring findings on all three grounds) and the exclusion of plans with fewer than 100 participants limited the retroactive bite, but the combination of a retroactive mandate, new civil penalties, and up to $5 billion in taxpayer-backed loans made the bill expensive and administratively heavy. A narrower, forward-looking version would have been easier to defend.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, and routed to a subcommittee, where it stayed with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 18, 2013 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.

On July 8, 2013 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions; the action history shows no hearing, markup, or vote at either level for the rest of the 113th Congress.
It never reached the House floor, and the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that had cut retiree health benefits keep the savings, and no future retirees get the protection the bill offered. Retirees who lost promised coverage get nothing.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor group was bipartisan — a Democrat (Tierney) with three original cosponsors including a Republican (Jones), and 2 of the 3 later cosponsors were Republicans — but the bill died in a Republican-held committee without a recorded vote, so no party split was ever measured.

industries.industry: Employers sponsoring retiree group health plans (large corporations and unions)
industries.note: The bill would force them to stop cutting retiree health coverage after retirement and to spend money restoring benefits already taken away, in some cases going back decades. It targeted a practice — reducing benefits to promised retirees who can no longer negotiate or switch jobs — that shifts health costs onto people with the least ability to bear them, so its financial interest ran directly against the retirees' interest.

The bill created a federal loan-guarantee program for employer loans of up to $5 billion through private lenders, a new government-backed line of business. It applied only if the bill's restoration mandate created demand for such loans, so the benefit was contingent on the bill's main provision taking effect.

industries.industry: Health insurers administering employer group plans
industries.note: Insurers would have to keep covering retiree populations that employers might otherwise have trimmed or shifted into cheaper managed-care arrangements, sustaining that premium revenue, while also administering restored benefit levels and any new plan provisions the law required.
